nodes.question: What technology is used for examining highly radioactive samples at Idaho National Laboratory?
nodes.answer: The Idaho National Laboratory uses laboratory-based micro-X-ray computed tomography for examining highly radioactive samples.
nodes.paragraph: IRRADIATION TESTING: FACILITIES, CAPABILITIES, AND EXPERIMENT DESIGNS Laboratory-Based Micro-X-ray Computed Tomography of Energy Materials at Idaho National Laboratory WILLIAM CHUIRAZZI ,1,2RAHUL REDDY KANCHARLA,1 and SWAPNIL MORANKAR1 1. Post-Irradiation Examination Department, Materials and Fuels Complex, Idaho National Laboratory, Idaho Falls, ID 83415, USA. 2. e-mail: william.chuirazzi@inl.gov The Idaho National Laboratory (INL) has implemented laboratory-based mi- cro-X-ray computed tomography in a laboratory equipped for the examinationof highly radioactive samples. This capability provides nondestructive three- dimensional volumetric information on samples to inform subsequent tradi- tional destructive examinations as well as real-world inputs for high- delityscienti C modeling. Samples can be imaged with spatial resolutions ranging from several hundred nm/voxel up to /C24100lm/voxel. The best usable spatial resolution achieved to date is 384 nm/voxel with this instrument, while thehighest radiological dose rate of a sample imaged is /C2460 R/h b/con contact. Advanced data analysis, including custom tomographic reconstruction and segmentation methods, have also been developed to support this capability. Inaddition to traditional digital X-ray radiography and tomography, thisinstrument is also able to visualize in situ tensile and compression testing as well as perform diffraction contrast tomography.

nodes.question: What types of examinations are performed during post-irradiation examination (PIE) at INL?
nodes.answer: PIE at INL includes nondestructive techniques like visual inspection and ultrasonics, semi-destructive examinations such as fission-gas sampling, and destructive examinations using methods like focused ion beam (FIB) and scanning electron microscope (SEM).
nodes.paragraph: Idaho National Laboratory (INL), founded in 1949 as heNational Reactor Testing Station, has the mission of discovering, demonstrating, and securing innova- tive nuclear energy solutions, other clean energyoptions, and critical infrastructure. As part of this mission space, post-irradiation examination (PIE) is performed on nuclear fuels and materials to mea-sure their performance and understand the mate-rial behaviors in the extreme temperature and radiation environments of a nuclear reactor. Traditional PIE activities 6include nondestructive techniques such as visual inspection and pro lom- etry,7,8ultrasonic thickness testing,9 11gamma-(Received April 29, 2024; accepted October 18, 2024; published online December 18, 2024)JOM, Vol. 77, No. 3, 2025 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-24-6970-z/C2112024 Battelle Energy Alliance, under exclusive licence to The Minerals, Metals & Materials Society 1337 emission scanning, 12neutron radiography13, 14and tomography, 15, 16some semi-destructive examina- tions such as ssion-gas sampling, 17as well as destructive examinations involving techniques such as focused ion beam (FIB), scanning electron micro- scope (SEM), transmission electron microscope(TEM), 18 23and thermal property measure- ments,24 26among others.

nodes.question: What techniques are used for the initial examination of irradiated materials at the HFEF?
nodes.answer: The initial examination at the HFEF is performed using nondestructive techniques.
nodes.paragraph: INL encompasses the full research and development cycle for nuclearmaterials, from conceptualizing and modeling of new fuel systems, to fabrication of novel fuels, fuel irradiation, and examination of the irradiated sam-ples to determine performance in extreme reactorenvironments, all to inform quali cation of safer and more ef cient nuclear fuels and materials. AT INL, the PIE work ow generally begins with shipping the irradiated material, whether from INL S Advanced Test Reactor 27or Transient Reactor Test Facility, 28, 29to the Material and Fuels Com- plex S (MFC) Hot Fuels Examination Facility (HFEF),30where they can undergo initial examina- tion within the hot cell, rst with nondestructivetechniques. The capabilities at MFC can examine highly radioactive samples from the engineering scale down to the langstrom scale. Once examina-tions at HFEF are complete, samples can be sec-tioned into smaller samples to isolate regions of interest and reduce the radiation dose rates before being repackaged and sent to other specializedexamination facilities. One of these facilities is the Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory (IMCL), which houses a variety of instruments forPIE for nuclear materials, including micro-X-ray computed tomography (XCT).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Industrial safety standards|Radiation safety protocols_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the purpose of using highly shielded containers for irradiated samples?
nodes.answer: The highly shielded containers are used to safely transfer irradiated samples into the facility and minimize radiation exposure to personnel during unloading and preparation.
nodes.paragraph: Irradiated samples are transferred into the facility in highlyshielded containers and unloaded from the contain- ers in the shielded sample preparation area remo- tely using manipulators. Samples can be remotelysectioned, polished, prepared, and mounted to min- imize radiation dose to personnel. If needed, sam- ples can undergo decontamination efforts in aradiological glovebox before being transferred to the laboratory. Instruments in IMCL consist of atom probe tomography, electron probe micro-analyzer, an X-ray diffractometer, FIB SEM, TEM, XCT, a nanoin- denter, and a suite of thermal properties instru- mentation (laser ash analyzer, simultaneousthermal analysis- mass spectrometry, thermal con- ductivity microscope, ash differential scanning calorimeter, and a physical property measurementsystem). Some of these instruments have a sample analysis station where instruments are coupled to a glovebox through a loading port. These gloveboxeshave shielded steel walls to minimize contamination and provide additional shielding of highly radioac- tive materials that are loaded into the instruments. X-ray Microscope A ZEISS Xradia 520 Versa X-ray Microscope (XRM) was installed in IMCL in 2019 to enable XCT examination of radioactive fuels and materials.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What doses of gamma irradiation were used in the study?
nodes.answer: The study used varying doses of gamma irradiation, specifically 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 Gray.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Maize is the third most important grain crop worldwide after wheat and rice; it is a vital global crop, serving as a key source of food, animal feed, and industrial products, making it essential for food security and economic stability in many countries. Drought stress adversely affects water uptake and can stunt growth, reducing the overall produc tivity of maize. So, this study was carried out to investigate the cytogenetic effects of gamma radiation and drought stress on maize SC131 genotype, focusing on chromosomal aberrations in seedling root meristems induced by vary ing doses of gamma irradiation (50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 Gray) and drought stress imposed by 10% polyethyl ene glycol (PEG). The present study also aims to evaluate the impact of these treatments on growth parameters under a controlled pot experiment. Additionally, molecular polymorphism induced by both gamma irradiation and drought stress was analyzed using Real Time quantitative PCR techniques for DREB2, ERF, and EF transcrip tion factors. Also, under a field condition experiment, maize plants were subjected to the same gamma irradiation doses and drought stress by reducing the number of irrigations, with subsequent evaluations of yield attributes to assess the overall impact of treatments on plant performance.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Industrial safety standards|Radiation safety protocols_qna_008
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What doses of gamma irradiation were applied during the experiment?
nodes.answer: The doses applied were 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 Gray.
nodes.paragraph: BMC Plant Biology (2025) 25:141 attributes of field-grown plants, (5) Study the SDS-PAGE banding pattern of yielded grains protein under the effect of gamma irradiation and drought treatments. Materials and methods Plant material and gamma irradiation Egyptian single cross of maize SC131 (Pedigree: Sakha9 X Sakha5) was used in this study. Grains of this geno - type was obtained from the Maize Research Depart - ment, Field Crops Research Institute of the Agricultural Research Center (ARC) in Giza, Egypt. This genotype was selected from the germplasm based on its agronomic importance as well as its disease-resistant and drought- tolerant properties. Grains were exposed to five doses of gamma irradiation using the Indian Gamma Cell Unit (IGCU) at the Atomic Energy Commission (AEC), Nasr City, Cairo, Egypt, using Co60 as a source of irradiation. The applied doses were 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 Gray (Dose Rate = 0.960 KGy/h). Grains of control samples were not exposed to gamma irradiation. Cytological procedures For the cytological analyses, two groups were used, first group comprised maize grains that were treated with gamma irradiation doses only and the second group that was treated with the same doses of radiation accompa - nied by the exposure to simulated drought using PEG- 6000 (10%).
